analogy.p: Imagine a restaurant kitchen shared by many chefs. Labelled jars (meaningful names), a recipe card for each dish (comments), a tidy layout with each station separate (indentation and structure) and standard sub-recipes such as 'make the sauce' that every dish reuses (subprograms) let any chef step in and cook without confusion, and changing the sauce recipe once changes every dish. The analogy breaks down because a kitchen with messy labels still produces food that tastes the same, whereas in code unclear structure also makes it far more likely that someone introduces a real error when editing.

bullets: **Maintainable** = easy to **read, understand, debug and modify** without breaking anything else.
The specification lists the techniques: **comments, indentation, meaningful (sensible) variable names and the use of subprograms**.
Maintainability does not change what the program does; it changes how easy the **source code** is for humans to work with.
It is a quality of the **source code**, so it is not visible to the end user running the program.
Part of **defensive design** because a program that is easy to fix and update stays reliable for longer.
Unmaintainable code is often called **spaghetti code**: tangled, uncommented, with unclear names.
core.p: **Maintainability** is how easy it is for a programmer to read, understand, correct and update a program after it has been written. In the OCR J277 specification it sits under defensive design (2.3), alongside anticipating misuse, validation and authentication. A maintainable program does not behave differently from an unmaintainable one: it produces the same output. The difference is for the people who work with the code later, who may be colleagues, the client's own team, or the original author coming back months afterwards and having forgotten how it works.

bullets: Programs are **updated and fixed after release**, so the code is read far more often than it is written.
Many programmers work on one project, so code must be **understandable by other people**.
Readable code makes **finding and fixing errors (debugging)** quicker, which saves time and money.
It makes it **safer to add new features**, because the programmer can see what each part does.
A programmer returning to their own code after months will have **forgotten the details**.
Maintainable code is easier to **test**, because each small part can be checked on its own.
Link to exam wording: say that it makes the code **easier to understand, debug and update**.
core.p: Real programs live for years. Bugs are found after release, laws and requirements change, operating systems are updated, and clients ask for new features. Every one of these jobs means somebody has to open the code and change it. If the code is hard to follow, each change takes far longer, costs more money and is more likely to introduce new errors. Large programs are written by teams, so people constantly read code that they did not write themselves.

bullets: A comment is **ignored by the translator** (compiler or interpreter) so it does not slow the program down or change its output.
OCR reference language: **// this is a comment**. In Python it is #.
Use comments to state the **purpose** of a subprogram, what its **parameters** are and what it **returns**.
Explain **why** something is done when it is not obvious, for example // minimum age set by law.
Comment **complicated sections**, such as nested loops or a calculation with several steps.
A comment such as // add 1 to x next to x = x + 1 is **pointless**: it repeats the code and adds nothing.
Comments must be **kept up to date**: a wrong comment is worse than none.
Exam point: comments help other programmers **understand what the code does** without reading every line.
core.p: A **comment** is text written in the source code that is ignored by the translator, so it has no effect on how the program runs. Its only job is to explain the code to a human reader. In the OCR reference language a comment starts with // and runs to the end of the line. Good comments explain what a block of code is for and why a decision was made, rather than repeating the code word for word. They are especially useful above subprograms, before complicated loops and next to important variables.

bullets: Indent everything **inside** an if, while, for or subprogram, and keep it consistent (for example 3 or 4 spaces).
Indentation shows **nesting**: a loop inside a loop, or an if inside a loop, is clear from the layout.
The closing keyword (endif, endwhile, next, endfunction) lines up with its **opening** keyword.
Use **blank lines** to separate logical blocks and subprograms.
Poor indentation makes it hard to see which lines are **inside the loop**, which causes logic errors.
Indentation is ignored by most languages' translators but is vital for **human readers**.
In an exam program, always indent: examiners can award marks only for code they can follow.
core.p: **Indentation** means moving lines of code to the right, usually by a fixed number of spaces, to show which statements belong inside a structure such as a loop, an IF statement or a subprogram. White space (blank lines and spaces) is used to separate sections. Indentation makes the structure visible at a glance, so a reader can see where a loop begins and ends and which lines are repeated. In Python, indentation is also part of the syntax, but in the OCR reference language it is a readability choice that the exam still expects you to use.

bullets: Choose names that describe the **purpose**: score, studentName, maxAttempts rather than s, n, m.
Be **consistent**: pick one convention (camelCase or snake_case) and stick to it in the whole program.
Subprograms should be named after what they **do**: calculateTotal(), validateAge(), displayMenu().
Avoid names that are **too short** (x) or **misleading** (a variable called total that holds an average).
Names cannot contain spaces and cannot start with a number, and should not be **reserved words** like if or while.
Use capitals for **constants** by convention, for example VAT_RATE.
Good names reduce the need for comments because the code **explains itself** (self-documenting).
Mark scheme wording: 'meaningful variable names so that the purpose of each variable is clear'.
core.p: A variable, constant, array or subprogram name is an **identifier**. A meaningful identifier describes what the item holds or does, so the code almost reads like English. Names such as a, b and x give no clue, while totalScore, passwordLength or calculateArea explain themselves. Programmers also follow a **naming convention**, an agreed pattern used throughout a project such as camelCase (firstName) or underscores (first_name), so names look consistent and are easy to recognise.

bullets: A subprogram is **written once and called many times**, so code is not repeated.
**Procedure**: procedure name(...) ... endprocedure. **Function**: function name(...) ... return value ... endfunction.
Breaking a large program into subprograms is called **modular programming** and links to decomposition.
If a bug is found, it is **fixed in one place** and every call to it is fixed too.
Short subprograms are easier to **read and test** than one huge block of code.
A good subprogram does **one job** and has a name that says what that job is.
Subprograms can be **reused** in other programs, saving development time.
They make a team project easier because different programmers can write **different subprograms**.
core.p: A **subprogram** is a named block of code that carries out one task and can be called from anywhere in the program. There are two kinds: a **procedure** carries out a task and does not have to return a value, while a **function** always returns a value to the place it was called from. Using subprograms is a major part of maintainable code because a long program is broken into small, self-contained parts. Each part can be understood, tested and corrected on its own.

bullets: A **parameter** is a value passed into a subprogram when it is called, for example calculateArea(length, width).
A **local variable** is declared inside a subprogram and can only be used there; a **global variable** is available everywhere.
Local variables reduce **accidental changes** and name clashes, so code is safer to edit.
A **constant** is given a value once and cannot change while the program runs: const VAT = 0.2.
Use a constant instead of typing the same value many times (a **magic number**): change it once and the whole program updates.
Passing data through parameters makes it clear **what each subprogram needs**.
Return values from functions make a subprogram **self-contained** and reusable.
Avoid too many global variables because any part of the program could change them, making bugs hard to trace.
core.p: Subprograms pass data in using **parameters**, and functions pass data back using the return value. Variables declared inside a subprogram are **local** and exist only while it runs, so a change inside one subprogram cannot accidentally alter a variable elsewhere. Constants hold values that never change, such as a VAT rate or a maximum number of attempts. Using these features together keeps the parts of a program independent, which means a change in one place does not break another.

bullets: Replace repeated lines with a **loop**, and repeated blocks with a **subprogram**.
A **magic number** is an unexplained value in the middle of code (0.2). Replace it with a named **constant** (DISCOUNT_RATE).
Arrays and loops are easier to maintain than variable1, variable2, variable3 and so on.
Copy-and-paste code means a **bug exists in many places**, but only some may get fixed.
Shorter, non-repetitive code is **less likely to contain errors**.
Changing a rule such as a pass mark should require **one edit**, not twenty.
Consistent structure means a new programmer knows **where to look** for each task.
core.p: If the same block of code is copied and pasted several times, then fixing a bug or changing a rule means finding and editing every copy, and it is easy to miss one. Programmers aim to write each piece of logic once. Repeating loops can replace repeated lines, subprograms can replace repeated blocks and constants can replace repeated numbers. This is often summed up as keeping code short, clear and in one place.

bullets: **Poor**: a = input() then b = a * 0.2: the reader cannot tell what a, b or 0.2 mean.
**Good**: price = input("Price") then discount = price * DISCOUNT_RATE: purpose is obvious.
Add a comment above: // work out the price after discount.
The output of both is **identical**; only readability and maintainability change.
In an exam, when asked to improve code, change **names, add comments, add indentation and extract subprograms**.
State what each change achieves, for example 'meaningful name so the reader knows it stores the price'.
Do not claim that maintainable code is **faster or uses less memory**: it is not about efficiency.
core.p: Looking at the same program written two ways shows the point of maintainability. In the poor version, the variable names are single letters, there are no comments, the layout is cramped and the number 0.2 appears without explanation. In the maintainable version, the code has a comment describing its purpose, names that explain themselves, a constant for the rate and clear indentation. A reader can understand the second version in seconds, and can safely change the discount in one place.

bullets: **Header comment** for each subprogram: purpose, inputs (parameters) and output (return value).
Comment **why**, not just what: // 3 attempts allowed to meet security policy.
Do not comment **obvious** lines; good names already explain them.
Update comments whenever the code changes, otherwise they become **misleading**.
Comments can **temporarily disable** code during testing (commenting out), but remove it in the final version.
In long exam answers, short comments show the examiner you **understand the logic**.
Comments are not a substitute for good names and structure; use **all the techniques together**.
core.h: Writing comments well: what, why and when
core.p: Not every line needs a comment, and over-commenting makes code harder to read. Good commenting follows a few habits. Begin each subprogram with a short header describing what it does, what goes in and what comes out. Comment blocks of code that do something non-obvious. Explain the reason for a decision, such as why a limit was chosen. Remove comments that are out of date, because misleading comments cause mistakes during later changes.

bullets: Link: **decomposition** breaks a problem into parts, which become subprograms.
Link: **testing**: small subprograms can be tested one at a time (iterative testing), then the whole program in final testing.
Link: the **IDE** has features such as code editors with auto-indentation and syntax highlighting that support readable code.
Link: **translators** ignore comments, so they do not affect speed or file size meaningfully.
Link: **validation and authentication** are the other two defensive design topics; maintainability is the third strand.
Higher-mark questions: always link a technique to its **benefit** (what it makes easier) and to **who benefits** (another programmer).
Distinguish: **maintainability** is about the source code; **usability** is about the user interface.
Do not confuse with **efficiency**, which is about speed and memory.
core.h: Maintainability, testing and the wider course
core.p: Maintainability links to many other parts of the J277 course. Decomposition and modular programming (from computational thinking) are what produce subprograms. Testing and debugging are much quicker when code is readable and split into small parts. Defensive design as a whole aims to make programs robust against misuse, errors and future change. Maintainability also depends on the translator: comments and white space are removed or ignored when the program is compiled or interpreted, so they cost nothing at run time.

bullets: Comments tell the reader the **purpose** of a section so they need not work it out line by line.
Indentation shows where loops, selections and subprograms start and end.
Meaningful names make the code read almost like a description of the problem.
A subprogram can be understood, changed and tested **on its own**.
Changing a named constant (such as VAT_RATE) updates every place it is used in one edit.
After any change the programmer re-tests the affected part and the programs that call it.
Maintainable code costs the client less because changes take less time.
The reader may be a colleague, a new employee or the original author months later.
core.h: Maintaining someone else's code: read, trace, change, test
core.p: When a programmer inherits a program they have never seen, the techniques in the specification decide how quickly they can work. They first **read** the code, using the comments to learn the purpose of each section and the meaningful names to see what each variable holds. They then **trace** the logic, using the indentation to see which statements belong to which loop or selection and the subprograms to follow one job at a time. Next they **change** the code in one place, and finally they **test** it to check that nothing else has broken. Poorly written code makes every one of these steps slower and riskier, which is why maintainability reduces cost for the organisation that owns the software.

bullets: Link every technique to a **benefit**: easier to read, understand, debug or update.
Comments: describe what the code does and why, in plain English.
Indentation: shows the structure and which lines are inside a loop or selection.
Meaningful names: show the purpose of each variable, such as totalScore, not x.
Subprograms: reuse, fix once, test separately, split the problem into manageable parts.
Do not say maintainable code is faster, shorter or uses less memory.
In your own Paper 2 programs, indent properly and choose sensible names every time.
For a rewrite question, show the improved code and label each change you made.
core.h: What to write in an exam answer on maintainability
core.p: Maintainability questions are marked on **technique plus benefit**, so every point should name a technique and then say what it makes easier for a programmer reading or changing the code. A good answer for comments is that they explain what the code does so that another programmer can understand it. A good answer for indentation is that it shows the structure of loops and selections, so the code is easier to follow and errors are easier to find. For subprograms the best marks go to saying that code can be reused, tested separately and corrected in one place. The wording should always refer to **readability and ease of change**, never to speed, memory or the size of the program.

exam: Maintainability questions are usually **2 to 6 marks**: 'State/Describe/Explain how X makes a program easier to maintain'.
Command words: **state** (one fact), **describe** (what it is), **explain** (technique plus benefit with a 'because').
The four techniques to learn: **comments, indentation, meaningful variable names, subprograms**.
For a 2-mark 'explain': name the technique (1) and say what it allows (1), for example 'comments explain what the code does so other programmers can understand it'.
For a 6-mark question, cover **at least three techniques**, each with a technique and a linked benefit, and write in full sentences.
Good model phrases: 'easier to understand', 'easier to debug', 'easier to update', 'code can be reused', 'fix it once'.
If given code to improve, **rewrite it** with names, comments, indentation and a constant, then label what you changed.
Never say it is 'faster', 'more efficient' or 'takes less memory': those marks are not awarded.
In your own programs in Paper 2, **always indent and use sensible names**; it helps you spot errors and examiners follow your logic.
Use the **OCR reference language** conventions: // for comments, procedure/function with end keywords.

mistakes.r: Maintainability makes code easier to read, debug and update; it does not change speed or memory use.
mistakes.w: Maintainable code runs faster or uses less memory.

mistakes.r: Comments are ignored by the translator; they only help human readers.
mistakes.w: Comments make the program do something extra when it runs.

mistakes.r: Indentation shows the structure (which lines are inside loops or selections), making the code easier to follow and debug.
mistakes.w: Writing 'it is neat' or 'it looks nice' for indentation.

mistakes.r: Use meaningful variable names that describe their purpose, such as totalScore.
mistakes.w: Using variable names like a, b and c in a program you write.

mistakes.r: Subprograms allow code to be reused, tested and fixed in one place, and they break the program into manageable parts.
mistakes.w: Saying subprograms make the program shorter only.

mistakes.r: Maintainability concerns the source code for programmers; usability concerns the interface for users.
Comment the purpose and complicated sections, and explain why, not just repeat the code.
mistakes.w: Commenting every single line, including obvious ones.

mistakes.r: Link each technique to the benefit: easier for another programmer to understand, debug or update.
mistakes.w: Describing a technique without saying what it makes easier.

mistakes.r: Break the program into subprograms that each do one job; this makes it easier to read, test and fix.
mistakes.w: Putting all of the code in one long block in the main program

summary: The specification asks you to know how code is made maintainable using comments, indentation, meaningful variable names and subprograms, and to explain why. It matters because real programs are changed for years by many different people, and you must also write readable code in the Paper 2 programming questions.

terms.d: How easy it is to read, understand, correct and update a program after it has been written.
Text in the source code that is ignored by the translator and explains the code to human readers.
Moving lines of code to the right to show which statements are inside a loop, selection or subprogram.
Blank lines and spaces used to separate sections of code and make it easier to read.
The name given to a variable, constant, array or subprogram.
An identifier that describes the purpose of the item, so the code is easy to understand.
An agreed style for writing identifiers consistently, such as camelCase.
A named value that is set once and cannot change while the program is running.
An unexplained value written directly in code, better replaced by a named constant.
A named block of code that performs a specific task and can be called from elsewhere in the program.
A subprogram that performs a task and does not have to return a value.
A subprogram that returns a value to the part of the program that called it.
A value passed into a subprogram when it is called.
A variable declared inside a subprogram that can only be used within that subprogram.
Dividing a program into separate subprograms (modules) that each do one job.
How easily a human can follow what the code does, helped by layout, names and comments.
The program as written by the programmer in a high-level language, before it is translated.
Tangled, uncommented code with unclear names and structure that is very hard to follow or change.
Finding and fixing the errors in a program.
Code written once in a subprogram and called whenever it is needed, instead of being copied.

worked.ans: Comments explain what the code does and why, so other programmers can understand it quickly. Meaningful variable names make the purpose of each variable clear, which makes the code easier to read, debug and update. Subprograms split the program into small parts that can be reused and tested separately, and because they are written once, a change or fix only needs to be made in one place.
worked.q: Explain how the use of comments, meaningful variable names and subprograms makes a program easier to maintain. [6]
steps: Comments (2): they describe what sections of code do and why, so another programmer can understand the code quickly without reading every line.
Meaningful variable names (2): names such as totalScore show the purpose of each variable, so the code is easier to read and mistakes are easier to spot when debugging.
Subprograms (2): code is split into named blocks that do one job, so each can be tested and corrected separately, and a bug fixed once is fixed everywhere the subprogram is called.

worked.ans:
const DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.2
// work out the price after discount
price = input("Price")
discount = price * DISCOUNT_RATE
salePrice = price - discount
print(salePrice)
worked.q:
Here is a program:
a = input("Price")
b = a * 0.2
c = a - b
print(c)
Rewrite it so that it is easier to maintain. [4]
steps: Rename the variables to describe their purpose: price, discount, salePrice (1 mark).
Replace 0.2 by a named constant such as DISCOUNT_RATE (1 mark).
Add at least one meaningful comment, for example // price after discount (1 mark).
Keep the program logic the same and lay it out clearly, one statement per line (1 mark).

worked.ans: Any error must be corrected in five places, and one might be missed; any change must be repeated five times. The code should be put into a subprogram (procedure or function) which is called each time it is needed.
worked.q: A programmer has copied the same 10 lines of code into five different places in a program. Give two reasons why this makes the program difficult to maintain and state one way to improve it. [3]
steps: If a bug is found, it must be fixed in all five places and one may be missed (1).
Any change to the rule must be repeated five times, which takes longer and risks inconsistency (1).
Improvement: put the 10 lines in a subprogram and call it five times (1).
